Chapter 2: The Limits of Reform and the Need for Revolution
Building on what we’ve already talked about—that the state is, at its core, a tool for class domination—let’s dig into a question that’s probably crossed your mind: can the state ever really be reformed to serve most people, instead of just a privileged few?
Over the years, plenty of passionate reformers and socialists have put their hope in gradual change. They’ve argued that through elections, new laws, and peaceful activism, we can turn the state into a force for justice and equality. Sounds reasonable, right? But here’s something to pay attention to—the state’s deep loyalty to those with power and wealth runs far deeper than most of us realize.
Imagine the state as a massive fortress, with thick stone walls and guards posted at every entrance. Reformers might change the color of the walls or swap out some of the guards, but the fortress itself? It still stands, protecting the same people it always has. The real machinery of government—its bureaucracy, the police, the military, the courts—has been carefully shaped over centuries to defend the interests of those who already hold the keys to the castle.
So, what happens when new leaders step in, full of good intentions? More often than not, they find themselves boxed in by these old structures. No matter how determined they are, they’re only able to make minor, surface-level changes.
That’s why, time after time, efforts at reform end up feeling like a letdown. Laws that are meant to protect workers or share wealth more fairly get watered down, blocked, or simply ignored. And when social movements start challenging the way things are, the state’s mask comes off. In moments of crisis, it doesn’t hesitate to drop any pretense of being neutral—it uses force to protect the old order.
Let me give you a few real-world examples to show how this plays out:
- Every time someone tries to pass a progressive law, entrenched interests inside the government dig in, making change feel almost impossible. - When regular people come together to demand something better, the state often pushes back hard—with violence or by tightening the law. - And even leaders who genuinely want to do the right thing quickly realize they have to keep the system stable and profitable for those at the top. All of this points to a tough but important truth: trying to turn the state into a real tool for democracy and equality—just by tinkering around the edges—won’t work. The way it’s built, from top to bottom, is meant to stop that kind of transformation from ever happening.
What does real change require? Not just another coat of paint or a new set of faces, but something much deeper—a revolution that takes apart the old machinery and builds something new from the ground up, with power truly rooted in the working class.
Now, when we talk about revolution, it’s not about seeking chaos or violence for its own sake. It’s about being honest: those with power aren’t going to just hand it over, and the state isn’t about to quietly step aside. If we want a society built on equality and real cooperation, we need to create new institutions that actually reflect what most people need and want.
So, here’s the key takeaway: the limits of reform aren’t just about the obstacles we see—they’re built right into the structure of the state itself. If we’re serious about changing the world, we have to recognize this reality, and be prepared to imagine—and fight for—more radical, lasting solutions.
